title: MicroRNA in Glioblastoma: Molecular Mechanisms, Clinical Relevance, and Therapeutic Opportunities

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Context of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
Glioblastoma is the most common and most malignant primary adult brain tumor, characterized by diffuse infiltration, rapid proliferation, necrosis, and microvascular proliferation. Integrated molecular profiling has shown that glioblastoma is not a single entity but a heterogeneous disease composed of transcriptional and genetic subtypes shaped by alterations in receptor tyrosine kinase, p53, and RB signaling networks, with frequent EGFR amplification, PTEN loss, and CDKN2A deletion ref [1], ref [2]. More recent single-cell analyses further demonstrated that substantial cellular plasticity coexists within individual tumors, with malignant cells transitioning among stem-like, progenitor-like, and mesenchymal states under microenvironmental and therapeutic pressures ref [3].

This intratumoral heterogeneity is compounded by a complex microenvironment that includes hypoxia, aberrant angiogenesis, immune suppression, and crosstalk with resident glia and infiltrating myeloid cells. Glioma stem-like cells are particularly important because they promote tumor propagation, adaptive resistance, and recurrence after therapy ref [4]. Clinically, maximal safe resection followed by radiotherapy and temozolomide remains the standard of care, yet survival gains have been modest; the landmark trial establishing this regimen still reported a median survival of only about 15 months ref [5].

A central clinical challenge is near-universal recurrence, driven by infiltrative cells that evade resection and by treatment-resistant subpopulations. MGMT promoter methylation provides a clinically relevant predictor of temozolomide benefit, but even molecularly stratified patients typically relapse ref [6]. The 2021 WHO classification has refined diagnostic criteria by integrating IDH status and other molecular features, underscoring that biologically informed subclassification is now essential for prognosis and therapeutic interpretation ref [7]. Together, these features make glioblastoma an especially compelling context in which to study microRNA-mediated regulation of invasion, stemness, and therapy response.

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Context of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: MicroRNA biogenesis and mechanisms of action
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are ~20–24 nucleotide regulatory RNAs generated through a stepwise biogenesis pathway that links nuclear RNA processing to cytoplasmic gene silencing. Canonical miRNA genes are transcribed mainly by RNA polymerase II as long primary transcripts (pri-miRNAs), which are cleaved in the nucleus by the Drosha–DGCR8 Microprocessor complex to yield precursor hairpins (pre-miRNAs). These are exported by Exportin-5 and further processed in the cytoplasm by Dicer to produce a duplex, one strand of which is preferentially loaded into an Argonaute-containing RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) ref [8], ref [9], ref [10].

Target recognition is driven primarily by complementarity between nucleotides 2–8 of the miRNA seed region and sequences enriched in 3′ untranslated regions of mRNAs. In animals, this interaction usually causes translational repression together with accelerated deadenylation and decay, allowing a single miRNA to coordinately modulate broad gene networks rather than acting as a simple on/off switch ref [11], ref [12]. Additional complexity arises from non-canonical biogenesis routes, context-dependent strand selection, and the integration of miRNAs into feedback loops with transcription factors, epigenetic regulators, and signaling pathways that shape cell identity and stress responses ref [9], ref [13].

These mechanistic features are especially relevant to glioblastoma, where modest changes in miRNA abundance can influence proliferation, stemness, invasion, apoptosis, and therapy resistance by simultaneously tuning multiple oncogenic and tumor-suppressive circuits. Because miRNAs function as network-level regulators and remain detectable in tissue and biofluids, their biogenesis and effector mechanisms provide the conceptual basis for both biomarker development and therapeutic targeting in this disease ref [13], ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Context of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: The regulatory landscape of non-coding RNAs in brain tumors
subsections.content:
Brain tumors are shaped by a multilayered non-coding RNA (ncRNA) network in which microRNAs interact with long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), circular RNAs (circRNAs), and other regulatory transcripts to control proliferation, invasion, stemness, and therapy response. Early transcriptomic studies established that both microRNA and lncRNA expression programs are extensively deregulated in gliomas, indicating that ncRNAs are integral components of the disease-defining molecular circuitry rather than passive transcriptional byproducts ref [15], ref [16].

Within this landscape, lncRNAs can function as scaffolds for chromatin regulators, modulators of transcription, or competitive endogenous RNAs that titrate microRNA availability. In glioblastoma, HOTAIR exemplifies oncogenic lncRNA activity through epigenetic reprogramming, whereas CRNDE is highly expressed in glioma and linked to growth-associated signaling states ref [17], ref [18]. CircRNAs add a further post-transcriptional layer through exceptional stability and context-dependent microRNA sequestration; broad analyses have highlighted their enrichment in neural tissues and their dysregulation in glioma, supporting their relevance to brain tumor biology ref [19].

This broader ncRNA framework is important for interpreting microRNA function in glioblastoma because regulatory effects are rarely linear. Instead, tumor phenotypes emerge from interconnected RNA networks that couple transcriptional control, RNA processing, and signal-dependent feedback. Integrative studies of glioblastoma transcriptomes have therefore emphasized ncRNA cross-talk as a source of molecular heterogeneity and as a potential reservoir of biomarkers and therapeutic vulnerabilities ref [16], ref [1].

subsections.section_title: Biological and Clinical Context of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Rationale for studying microRNA in glioblastoma
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs are compelling targets in glioblastoma because they sit at a regulatory level capable of integrating oncogenic signaling, lineage state, and stress adaptation. Their aberrant expression is pervasive in gliomas and often maps onto core malignant phenotypes, including uncontrolled proliferation, diffuse invasion, stem-like self-renewal, and resistance to apoptosis. Early profiling studies showed that glioblastoma exhibits reproducible microRNA dysregulation relative to normal brain, nominating specific oncogenic and tumor-suppressive microRNAs as components of disease-defining networks rather than passive biomarkers ref [15], ref [20].

The rationale is strengthened by functional evidence that individual microRNAs can control clinically relevant pathways converging on EGFR, PTEN/PI3K/AKT, cell-cycle regulators, and differentiation programs. Canonical examples include miR-21, which promotes survival and therapeutic resistance, and miR-10b, which supports glioma cell growth and invasion, whereas miR-34a and miR-128 act as tumor suppressors linked to stem-cell regulation and impaired proliferation when restored ref [21], ref [22], ref [23], ref [24]. Because each microRNA can coordinately repress many transcripts, microRNA perturbation may reveal network vulnerabilities that are difficult to capture through single-gene analysis.

MicroRNAs are also attractive from a translational perspective. They are measurable in tissue and biofluids, show relative molecular stability, and may assist in subclassification, prognosis, and response monitoring. In parallel, therapeutic strategies based on microRNA inhibition or replacement are conceptually suited to glioblastoma, where pathway redundancy and intratumoral heterogeneity often undermine narrowly targeted agents ref [25]. Thus, studying microRNAs offers both mechanistic insight into glioblastoma biology and a practical framework for developing multi-target biomarkers and interventions.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation and Oncogenic Networks in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
A subset of microRNAs is consistently overexpressed in glioblastoma and functions as bona fide oncomiRs by enhancing proliferation, survival, invasion, and therapeutic resistance. Among these, miR-21 is the most reproducibly upregulated species in malignant glioma, where it suppresses multiple pro-apoptotic and growth-restraining targets and thereby promotes tumor cell viability and resistance to cell death ref [26], ref [27]. miR-10b is also aberrantly expressed in glioblastoma despite being largely absent from normal brain; its inhibition impairs glioma growth and survival, supporting a lineage-inappropriate but functionally important oncogenic role ref [28].

Other tumor-promoting microRNAs reinforce core glioblastoma signaling networks. miR-221 and miR-222 drive cell-cycle progression and proliferation in part through repression of the CDK inhibitors p27Kip1 and p57, linking their overexpression to unchecked mitogenic signaling ref [29]. miR-26a, frequently amplified together with oncogenic loci in high-grade glioma, contributes to transformation by targeting PTEN and cooperating with other genomic alterations to activate PI3K/Akt signaling ref [30]. In parallel, miR-93 has been implicated in promoting angiogenesis and tumor expansion, highlighting how oncomiRs can support both cancer cell-intrinsic and microenvironmental programs ref [31].

Collectively, these studies indicate that glioblastoma oncomiRs rarely act through a single target; instead, they coordinately dampen apoptosis, strengthen growth-factor signaling, accelerate cell-cycle transit, and facilitate invasion or vascular remodeling. This network-level mode of action helps explain why recurrent overexpression of a relatively small set of microRNAs can exert broad oncogenic effects in glioblastoma biology ref [26], ref [28], ref [30], ref [31].

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation and Oncogenic Networks in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
A substantial subset of glioblastoma-associated microRNAs acts in a tumor-suppressive manner and is frequently downregulated relative to normal brain. Among the best characterized is miR-7, which restrains epidermal growth factor receptor signaling and downstream Akt activity, thereby reducing proliferation and invasiveness in glioblastoma cells ref [32]. Likewise, miR-34a is commonly diminished in glioblastoma and suppresses growth-promoting programs by targeting receptor tyrosine kinase and cell-cycle networks, including c-Met and Notch pathway components ref [33]. These studies established that loss of specific microRNAs can release multiple oncogenic nodes simultaneously, a feature particularly relevant in highly heterogeneous tumors.

Other tumor-suppressive microRNAs converge on cell-cycle progression, apoptosis resistance, and stemness. miR-128 is reduced in gliomas and inhibits self-renewal and proliferation through targets such as Bmi-1, linking microRNA loss to maintenance of stem-like phenotypes ref [34]. miR-137 similarly promotes differentiation and cell-cycle arrest in glioblastoma by repressing Cdk6, supporting a role in opposing undifferentiated tumor states ref [35]. The brain-enriched miR-124 also suppresses glioma growth and promotes neuronal differentiation programs, in part through inhibition of STAT3 signaling and related oncogenic transcriptional outputs ref [36].

Additional suppressive circuits include miR-181 family members and miR-326, both of which are frequently attenuated in glioblastoma. Reduced miR-181 expression has been associated with impaired apoptotic responsiveness and adverse biology, whereas restoration of miR-326 limits tumorigenicity by repressing Notch signaling and related survival pathways ref [37], ref [38]. Collectively, tumor-suppressive microRNAs in glioblastoma function less as isolated regulators than as multilayered buffers of oncogenic networks; their loss therefore amplifies signaling plasticity, stem-cell maintenance, and treatment resistance.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation and Oncogenic Networks in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
MicroRNA dysregulation in glioblastoma arises from convergent genetic, epigenetic, and transcriptional disturbances. Copy-number changes and locus-specific alterations can directly affect miRNA abundance, but a major layer of control is aberrant transcriptional regulation by oncogenic signaling networks. In particular, EGFR/RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT activity feeds into transcription factors such as c-Myc and NF-κB that broadly remodel miRNA programs, while p53 loss removes an important tumor-suppressive input on multiple miRNAs, including the miR-34 family ref [26], ref [39]. TGF-β signaling also contributes to context-dependent repression or induction of miRNA expression in high-grade glioma cells ref [40].

Epigenetic silencing is another prominent upstream mechanism. Promoter CpG hypermethylation suppresses several tumor-suppressive miRNAs in glioblastoma, including miR-124 and miR-137, linking altered DNA methylation to maintenance of an undifferentiated, proliferative state ref [41]. Polycomb-associated chromatin repression likewise shapes the glioma miRNA landscape; EZH2-mediated H3K27 trimethylation can suppress differentiation-associated miRNAs and reinforce stem-like phenotypes ref [42]. These observations place miRNA dysregulation within the broader epigenomic abnormalities that typify IDH-wild-type glioblastoma.

Beyond transcription and chromatin, defects in miRNA biogenesis may further distort expression patterns. Core processing components such as Drosha and Dicer are frequently altered across cancers and can globally affect mature miRNA output ref [43]. In glioblastoma specifically, hypoxia is an important microenvironmental upstream cue, inducing HIF-dependent miRNAs such as miR-210 and thereby coupling oxygen stress to adaptive gene-expression programs relevant to angiogenesis, survival, and treatment resistance ref [44]. Together, these mechanisms explain why miRNA alterations in glioblastoma are coordinated network-level consequences of oncogenic state rather than isolated expression changes.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation and Oncogenic Networks in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: MicroRNA-target gene interactions and pathway regulation
subsections.content:
In glioblastoma, microRNAs shape malignant behavior by coordinately repressing nodal effectors rather than single genes, thereby remodeling signaling networks that control proliferation, invasion, apoptosis, and therapy response. A canonical example is miR-21, which is consistently overexpressed and suppresses multiple tumor-suppressive targets, including PDCD4, TPM1, and components of apoptotic programs, linking microRNA dysregulation to enhanced survival and invasiveness in glioma cells ref [45]. Conversely, loss of tumor-suppressive microRNAs derepresses oncogenic pathways: miR-7 targets EGFR and downstream Akt signaling, and its restoration attenuates growth and viability in glioblastoma models ref [32].

Several glioblastoma-relevant microRNAs converge on the PI3K/Akt, RAS/MAPK, and receptor tyrosine kinase axes. miR-34a directly represses c-Met, Notch1/2, and CDK6, thereby integrating control of mitogenic signaling with cell-cycle progression and stem-like traits ref [46]. The miR-128 family similarly constrains self-renewal and proliferation by targeting Bmi-1 and E2F3a, illustrating how microRNAs connect epigenetic regulators to proliferative transcriptional programs ref [24]. In parallel, miR-181 family members have been reported to suppress KPNA4 and other effectors associated with invasion and malignant progression, supporting a broader role for microRNAs in rewiring migratory circuitry ref [47].

Network-level regulation is also evident in the p53 pathway and mesenchymal transition. miR-221/222 promote glioblastoma growth by repressing the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors p27 and p57, reinforcing cell-cycle entry and treatment resistance ref [48]. By contrast, miR-10b, although better known as an oncomiR, exemplifies how a single microRNA can influence diverse downstream targets that collectively sustain proliferation and invasion; its inhibition impairs glioma cell survival in part through derepression of cell-cycle and pro-apoptotic regulators ref [49]. Together, these studies indicate that microRNA-target interactions in glioblastoma are best understood as multiplex regulatory modules that stabilize oncogenic pathway states.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation and Oncogenic Networks in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: MicroRNA control of glioblastoma stem-like cells
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs are integral regulators of the glioblastoma stem-like cell (GSC) state, shaping self-renewal, multipotency, tumor initiation, and therapeutic resistance. Early profiling studies showed that the neural differentiation-associated miR-124 and miR-137 are markedly reduced in high-grade gliomas and that their re-expression induces cell-cycle arrest and neuronal differentiation programs, arguing that loss of these microRNAs helps preserve stem-like phenotypes in malignant cells ref [1]. In parallel, miR-34a functions as a key brake on stemness-linked signaling by targeting oncogenic effectors including c-Met and Notch pathway components, thereby limiting clonogenic growth and tumor propagation ref [2].

Several microRNAs act more directly on the GSC transcriptional circuitry. miR-128 is commonly suppressed in glioblastoma and inhibits self-renewal by targeting Bmi-1, a Polycomb regulator required for neural and glioma stem cell maintenance ref [3]. Likewise, the miR-302-367 cluster has been shown to repress stem-like traits and glioma-initiating capacity through coordinated inhibition of CXCR4 and related self-renewal networks ref [4]. These findings support a model in which loss of differentiation-promoting microRNAs and enrichment of stemness-permissive programs cooperate to stabilize the GSC compartment.

Conversely, specific oncomiRs reinforce GSC survival. miR-21, one of the most consistently upregulated microRNAs in glioblastoma, promotes anti-apoptotic and invasive phenotypes and has been implicated in maintenance of tumor-initiating populations ref [5]. More broadly, integrated analyses of GSCs have identified microRNA signatures linked to core stem-cell pathways such as Notch, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, and epigenetic regulation, highlighting microRNA networks as both markers of GSC heterogeneity and candidate therapeutic nodes ref [6].

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA Dysregulation and Oncogenic Networks in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
MicroRNA-mediated communication between glioblastoma cells and the tumor microenvironment is increasingly recognized as a bidirectional determinant of malignancy. Glioblastoma-derived extracellular vesicles shuttle selected microRNAs to endothelial, immune, and stromal cells, thereby reshaping angiogenesis, inflammation, and niche support. A prominent example is exosomal miR-21, which is abundant in cerebrospinal fluid and tumor-derived vesicles and reflects active exchange between tumor cells and surrounding compartments ref [50]. More broadly, extracellular vesicle transfer from glioblastoma alters recipient-cell transcriptional programs and supports a microenvironment permissive for invasion and treatment resistance ref [51].

Specific microRNAs also link glioblastoma cells to hypoxic and vascular niches. Hypoxia induces miR-210, a canonical stress-responsive microRNA that coordinates adaptation to low oxygen and promotes angiogenic remodeling, thereby reinforcing survival in poorly perfused tumor regions ref [52]. In parallel, glioblastoma-secreted vesicles can deliver pro-angiogenic signals, including microRNA cargo, to endothelial cells; Skog and colleagues showed that tumor microvesicles transfer RNA species that stimulate angiogenic behavior and can be detected in patient circulation ref [53]. These findings place microRNAs among the effectors through which neoplastic cells condition the perivascular niche.

MicroRNAs further participate in immune crosstalk, especially in the education of tumor-associated macrophages and microglia. A notable mechanism involves glioblastoma exosomal miR-1246, which drives macrophage polarization toward an immunosuppressive phenotype that favors tumor growth ref [54]. Conversely, microenvironmental signals can remodel microRNA expression in tumor cells; for example, mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes suppress glioma xenograft growth partly through delivery of miR-124 and miR-145, illustrating that stromal microRNAs may also exert tumor-restraining effects ref [6]. Together, these studies support a model in which microRNAs function not only as intracellular regulators but also as intercellular signals integrating glioblastoma with its vascular and immune milieu.

subsections.section_title: Functional Roles of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma Progression and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.subsection_title: Regulation of proliferation, apoptosis, and cell-cycle progression
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs are central post-transcriptional regulators of glioblastoma growth because they coordinately tune oncogenic signaling, apoptosis, and checkpoint control. A recurrent theme is loss of tumor-suppressive miRNAs that normally restrain receptor tyrosine kinase and PI3K/AKT output. Among the best characterized examples, miR-7 is frequently reduced in glioblastoma and suppresses EGFR and components of the Akt pathway, thereby limiting proliferation and clonogenicity ref [55]. Similarly, miR-34a is commonly downregulated, particularly in p53-altered contexts, and inhibits growth by targeting c-Met, Notch, and CDK6-linked programs that support cell-cycle progression and survival ref [56].

Other miRNAs directly couple proliferative control to apoptotic competence. miR-128 is diminished in high-grade gliomas and targets Bmi-1 and E2F3a, promoting G1 restraint and reducing self-renewal and tumor growth ref [24]. In contrast, the oncomiR miR-21 is consistently overexpressed in glioblastoma, where it suppresses multiple pro-apoptotic and antiproliferative effectors and thereby enhances cell survival while reducing caspase-dependent death ref [57]. miR-221/222 similarly drive proliferation by repressing the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p27Kip1, linking miRNA dysregulation to accelerated cell-cycle transit ref [58].

Additional tumor-suppressive nodes include miR-137 and miR-124, which are associated with neural differentiation and inhibit glioma cell proliferation through effects on CDK6 and related cell-cycle machinery ref [59], ref [60]. Collectively, these studies indicate that glioblastoma expansion is not governed by single miRNA lesions, but by a rewired miRNA network that simultaneously disables apoptosis, shortens G1 control, and amplifies mitogenic signaling.

subsections.section_title: Functional Roles of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma Progression and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.subsection_title: Invasion, migration, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal-like transition programs
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs are central regulators of the highly infiltrative phenotype of glioblastoma, in part by tuning cytoskeletal remodeling, extracellular-matrix interaction, and mesenchymal state transitions. Among the best-studied examples, miR-21 promotes invasion and migration by suppressing multiple anti-invasive restraints, including RECK and TIMP3, thereby favoring matrix metalloproteinase activity and tissue infiltration in glioma cells ref [61]. Conversely, several tumor-suppressive microRNAs are lost during progression, releasing pro-migratory transcriptional and signaling programs.

A prominent anti-invasive network is formed by miR-34a, miR-124, and miR-137. miR-34a is reduced in glioblastoma and constrains motility partly through targeting oncogenic effectors such as c-Met and Notch-associated pathways ref [62]. miR-124 and miR-137, two neuronally enriched microRNAs frequently suppressed in high-grade glioma, inhibit migration while promoting a more differentiated state, linking lineage commitment to reduced dispersal capacity ref [63]. Similarly, miR-10b, which is largely absent from normal brain but elevated in gliomas, supports invasion and viability, reinforcing its role as a glioma-specific driver of aggressive behavior ref [22].

MicroRNAs also intersect with epithelial-to-mesenchymal-like programs characteristic of the mesenchymal glioblastoma subtype. The miR-200 family, canonical antagonists of EMT through ZEB1/2 repression in epithelial cancers, is generally low in glioblastoma and has been shown to suppress glioma cell migration and stem-like traits when restored ref [64]. In parallel, mesenchymal transition can be reinforced by inflammatory signaling circuits involving miR-221/222, which enhance proliferation and invasiveness through repression of cell-cycle and motility regulators ref [65]. Collectively, these data position microRNAs as nodal determinants of glioblastoma dissemination and state plasticity, with direct relevance to local recurrence after therapy.

subsections.section_title: Functional Roles of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma Progression and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs are integral to the angiogenic circuitry of glioblastoma, where hypoxia-inducible programs couple vascular remodeling to tumor adaptation. A central example is miR-210, a canonical hypoxia-responsive microRNA induced by HIF signaling that promotes endothelial cell migration and capillary formation and has been linked to poor outcome in glioma, consistent with a role in sustaining the hypoxic, proangiogenic niche ref [66]. Glioblastoma-associated endothelial interactions are also influenced by miR-296, which is induced by angiogenic growth factors and enhances neovascularization by increasing VEGFR2 and PDGFRβ abundance through suppression of HGS-mediated receptor degradation ref [67]. In parallel, loss of anti-angiogenic microRNAs can reinforce VEGF output; miR-128 is reduced in glioma and directly represses p70S6K1, thereby dampening HIF-1α and VEGF signaling ref [24].

Metabolic reprogramming in glioblastoma is likewise shaped by microRNAs that connect glycolysis, mitochondrial function, and stress tolerance. miR-451 acts as a metabolic rheostat: under glucose-replete conditions it supports proliferation through the LKB1/AMPK pathway, whereas reduced miR-451 during metabolic stress facilitates adaptation and survival, linking nutrient sensing to phenotypic plasticity ref [68]. Broader hypoxic adaptation also involves miR-210, which suppresses mitochondrial respiration and favors glycolytic metabolism, reinforcing the glycolytic switch characteristic of aggressive tumors ref [69]. In addition, the glioma-enriched miR-21 contributes to anabolic and survival signaling, in part by promoting PI3K/Akt pathway activity through repression of tumor suppressive targets, thereby indirectly supporting the metabolic state associated with rapid growth and therapy resistance ref [70]. Together, these data position microRNAs as nodal regulators that synchronize angiogenesis with bioenergetic rewiring in glioblastoma.

subsections.section_title: Functional Roles of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma Progression and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs are central modulators of glioblastoma chemosensitivity, particularly in the response to temozolomide (TMZ). A recurrent theme is regulation of DNA damage repair and apoptotic threshold. miR-21, one of the most consistently upregulated oncomiRs in glioblastoma, promotes resistance to cytotoxic therapies by suppressing pro-apoptotic signaling and enhancing survival networks; its inhibition increases treatment responsiveness in glioblastoma models ref [71]. Conversely, several tumor-suppressive miRNAs restore TMZ sensitivity. miR-181d directly downregulates MGMT, providing a mechanistic link between miRNA expression and the major determinant of TMZ resistance ref [72].

Additional miRNAs converge on DNA repair, stem-like persistence, and prosurvival signaling. miR-603 was shown to suppress IGF1/IGF1R signaling and MGMT, and radiation-induced export of miR-603 through extracellular vesicles promoted a resistant, stem-cell-like state, illustrating how stress responses can secondarily reinforce chemotherapy resistance ref [73]. miR-195, together with miR-455-3p, also targets MGMT and contributes to epigenetic and post-transcriptional control of TMZ response ref [74]. In parallel, miR-10b supports glioblastoma cell survival and therapeutic resistance, and antagonizing miR-10b reduces viability of tumor cells while sparing normal neural cells, highlighting its translational appeal ref [75].

Resistance is further shaped by exosome-mediated transfer of miRNAs within the tumor microenvironment. Exosomal miR-1238 has been implicated in the horizontal propagation of TMZ resistance among glioblastoma cells through activation of CAV1/EGFR-linked signaling ref [76]. Collectively, these studies indicate that miRNAs influence TMZ efficacy at multiple levels—MGMT expression, apoptotic competence, adaptive stress signaling, and intercellular communication—supporting miRNA-based stratification and combination strategies to overcome chemotherapy resistance.

subsections.section_title: Functional Roles of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma Progression and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.content:
MicroRNAs are increasingly implicated in the adaptive response of glioblastoma to ionizing radiation, particularly through control of DNA-damage signaling, apoptosis, and stem-like cell survival. A recurrent theme is the enrichment of oncogenic miRNAs after irradiation and in radioresistant models. For example, miR-21, one of the best-characterized glioblastoma oncomiRs, attenuates radiation-induced apoptosis and promotes survival signaling, while its inhibition enhances radiosensitivity ref [77]. Similarly, hypoxia-responsive miR-210 links the irradiated microenvironment to stress adaptation by supporting survival under low-oxygen conditions, a state tightly associated with radioresistance in glioblastoma ref [78].

Other miRNAs appear to act as radiosensitizers by restraining checkpoint activation or repair capacity. miR-181a has been reported to increase radiation responsiveness in glioma cells by facilitating apoptosis and limiting pro-survival pathways ref [79]. In parallel, miR-100 suppresses DNA repair-related signaling and sensitizes tumor-initiating or stem-like glioblastoma cells to irradiation, underscoring how miRNA networks intersect with the treatment-refractory stem-cell compartment ref [80]. These observations are consistent with broader evidence that glioma stem cells preferentially activate DNA damage checkpoints after radiation, thereby sustaining clonogenic recovery ref [81].

Stress adaptation after radiotherapy also extends beyond cell-intrinsic repair to intercellular communication. Extracellular vesicle-associated miRNAs can remodel recipient-cell behavior and may propagate resistant phenotypes within the tumor niche. In this context, exosomal transfer of miR-301a under hypoxia has been shown to promote radioresistance through Wnt/beta-catenin pathway activation ref [82]. Collectively, these data support a model in which miRNAs integrate hypoxic stress, DNA-damage responses, and stemness programs, making them attractive candidates for radiosensitizing combination strategies in glioblastoma.

subsections.section_title: Functional Roles of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma Progression and Therapeutic Resistance
subsections.content:
Glioblastoma recurrence reflects Darwinian selection imposed by surgery, radiation, and temozolomide, together with marked spatial and temporal intratumoral heterogeneity. Longitudinal genomic analyses have shown that recurrent tumors often retain an ancestral trunk but acquire divergent subclones and therapy-associated alterations, indicating that relapse is an evolutionary process rather than simple regrowth of the primary lesion ref [83], ref [84]. In this setting, microRNAs are well positioned to act as rapid post-transcriptional regulators of adaptive states, because they can simultaneously tune stemness, DNA-damage responses, and survival pathways that become enriched after treatment.

Several microRNAs have been directly linked to glioblastoma stem-like persistence and recurrence-prone phenotypes. miR-21, one of the most consistently upregulated glioblastoma miRNAs, promotes anti-apoptotic signaling and treatment tolerance, features compatible with survival of residual disease ref [27]. By contrast, miR-128 suppresses self-renewal and stem-cell programs through targets including Bmi-1, suggesting that loss of miR-128 may favor repopulation after therapy ref [34]. miR-34a also restrains proneural/stem-like traits by targeting pathways such as Notch and c-Met; its depletion therefore supports plasticity and tumor re-initiation ref [85]. In parallel, hypoxia-inducible miR-210 links microenvironmental stress to adaptive survival, a relevant mechanism in the irradiated and ischemic post-treatment bed ref [86].

Recurrence is also shaped by intercellular communication. Glioblastoma-derived extracellular vesicles carry oncogenic microRNAs that can remodel neighboring tumor and stromal cells, potentially propagating resistant programs after therapy ref [50]. Overall, available evidence supports a model in which recurrent evolution is driven not only by genetic selection but also by microRNA-mediated state transitions, preserving a reservoir of stem-like, stress-adapted cells that fuel relapse.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA as Diagnostic, Prognostic, and Predictive Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
Tumor tissue profiling first established that glioblastoma harbors reproducible microRNA abnormalities relative to non-neoplastic brain. Early expression studies identified marked upregulation of oncogenic miRNAs such as miR-21 and downregulation of neural/tumor-suppressive species including miR-128 and miR-181 family members, supporting the concept that tissue miRNA signatures capture both lineage state and malignant transformation ref [15], ref [87]. Integrative analyses further linked deregulated miRNAs to core glioblastoma pathways, including EGFR/PI3K/AKT, p53, and mesenchymal transition programs ref [2].

Beyond tumor-versus-normal discrimination, tissue miRNA patterns have shown value for molecular stratification. Distinct signatures have been associated with proneural, classical, and mesenchymal phenotypes and with IDH-mutant versus IDH-wildtype diffuse gliomas, indicating that miRNA readouts can complement transcriptomic subclassification and reflect underlying biology ref [2], ref [88]. Functionally, several highly expressed tissue miRNAs are not merely correlates but candidate drivers: miR-21 promotes invasion and apoptosis resistance, whereas miR-10b supports proliferation and survival in glioma cells ref [26], ref [89].

However, the translational use of tumor tissue miRNA signatures remains constrained by intratumoral heterogeneity, differences between bulk and microdissected specimens, and sensitivity to platform and normalization choices. Comparative analyses also suggest that formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue can preserve miRNAs reasonably well, which is advantageous for retrospective biomarker studies, but robust cross-cohort validation is still needed before routine clinical adoption ref [90].

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA as Diagnostic, Prognostic, and Predictive Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
Circulating microRNAs have attracted particular interest in glioblastoma because they offer a minimally invasive window into an anatomically inaccessible tumor. Early studies showed that serum miR-21 is elevated in patients with glioblastoma and decreases after surgery, supporting its potential utility for disease detection and longitudinal monitoring, although overlap with inflammatory and other neoplastic conditions limits its specificity ref [91]. Broader plasma or serum profiling has further identified dysregulated species such as miR-128 and miR-342-3p, suggesting that multi-analyte signatures may outperform single-marker approaches for distinguishing glioblastoma from non-neoplastic controls ref [92].

Extracellular vesicles, especially exosomes, are especially relevant because they protect microRNAs from degradation and are actively released by glioma cells into biofluids. Glioblastoma-derived microvesicles were shown to carry tumor-specific RNA cargo, establishing the biological basis for liquid biopsy approaches in this disease ref [50]. Subsequent work demonstrated that serum exosomal microRNA panels can discriminate glioblastoma patients from healthy individuals with relatively high accuracy, with recurrent involvement of miR-21, miR-222, and related oncogenic microRNAs ref [93]. Cerebrospinal fluid may provide an even more tumor-proximal compartment, and extracellular vesicle analysis from CSF has revealed glioblastoma-associated RNA signatures that may complement blood-based assays ref [94].

Despite these advances, translation remains constrained by pre-analytical and analytical variability, including differences in serum versus plasma processing, hemolysis, vesicle isolation methods, and normalization strategies. Large systematic analyses indicate that blood-derived RNA profiles can be dominated by exRNA from hematopoietic cells and platelets, complicating attribution to the tumor unless rigorously controlled ref [95]. Accordingly, the most promising clinical direction is likely standardized, longitudinal assessment of composite circulating and extracellular vesicle-associated microRNA signatures integrated with imaging and molecular context rather than reliance on any single biomarker.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA as Diagnostic, Prognostic, and Predictive Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
Prognostic microRNA panels in glioblastoma have been pursued to move beyond single-marker associations toward more robust risk stratification. Early large-cohort analyses showed that recurrent expression patterns, rather than individual microRNAs alone, better captured survival heterogeneity; notably, a ten-microRNA profile was reported to stratify glioblastoma patients into distinct outcome groups and to retain prognostic value alongside established clinicopathologic variables ref [96]. This panel-based logic is biologically plausible because microRNAs regulate convergent networks governing proliferation, invasion, stemness, hypoxia adaptation, and apoptosis.

Subsequent studies refined this concept by integrating microRNA signatures with molecular subclassification and treatment context. In particular, Srinivasan et al. identified a microRNA expression signature associated with survival and glioblastoma subtype, supporting the view that prognostic panels may partly reflect underlying lineage states and oncogenic circuitry ref [15]. Other work highlighted recurrent adverse associations for mesenchymal- or invasion-linked microRNAs such as miR-196 and favorable associations for neuronal differentiation-related microRNAs, although reproducibility across cohorts has been inconsistent ref [97], ref [2].

Despite promising retrospective findings, few prognostic panels have reached clinical implementation. Major obstacles include small discovery sets, platform-dependent normalization, intratumoral heterogeneity, and confounding by IDH status, MGMT promoter methylation, and extent of resection. Studies using standardized resources such as TCGA have improved analytical rigor, but external validation remains limited ref [1], ref [6]. Consequently, the most credible near-term role for microRNA panels is likely as complementary prognostic layers within integrated models rather than as stand-alone survival predictors.

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA as Diagnostic, Prognostic, and Predictive Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
A major goal in glioblastoma biomarker research is to identify microRNAs that predict benefit from radiotherapy and temozolomide rather than merely correlate with outcome. Mechanistically, several miRNAs modulate DNA damage responses, apoptosis, stemness, and MGMT-associated resistance pathways, making them plausible predictive markers. Among the best studied, miR-21 promotes treatment resistance through anti-apoptotic signaling and was shown to influence chemosensitivity in glioblastoma models ref [98]. Conversely, restoration of miR-181d suppresses MGMT expression, linking this miRNA to temozolomide responsiveness and suggesting utility beyond MGMT promoter methylation alone ref [47].

Other candidate predictive miRNAs converge on radioresistance and invasive recurrence. miR-10b is highly expressed in glioblastoma and supports tumor growth and survival, providing a rationale for its association with resistance phenotypes and for therapeutic targeting ref [99]. miR-195, miR-455-3p, and related species have also been implicated in modulating response through effects on cell-cycle control, hypoxia signaling, and stem-like states, although reproducibility across cohorts remains limited. Importantly, miRNA effects are often context dependent, varying with IDH status, MGMT methylation, and transcriptomic subtype.

These observations support the use of composite miRNA panels, integrated with established molecular markers, to predict treatment response more robustly than single analytes. However, most studies remain retrospective and underpowered, with heterogeneous sampling times and endpoints. Prospective validation in uniformly treated cohorts, ideally using matched tissue and liquid biopsy specimens, will be necessary before miRNA-based predictive assays can inform patient selection for alkylating chemotherapy, radiosensitization strategies, or experimental targeted therapies ref [100], ref [101], ref [102].

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA as Diagnostic, Prognostic, and Predictive Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Integration with multi-omics and precision oncology
subsections.content:
Integrating microRNA data with genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic layers is increasingly central to precision oncology in glioblastoma. Early multidimensional profiling established that glioblastoma comprises biologically distinct transcriptional subtypes linked to characteristic driver alterations, providing a framework in which microRNAs can be interpreted as regulators and readouts of subtype-specific circuitry rather than isolated biomarkers ref [1]. Large-scale integrative analyses further showed that copy-number change, mutation, DNA methylation, mRNA expression, and microRNA abundance jointly define tumor states and clinically relevant heterogeneity ref [2].

Within this framework, several microRNAs have been mapped onto actionable pathways. For example, mesenchymal transition and NF-κB/C/EBP signaling are reinforced by regulatory networks in which non-coding RNAs participate, suggesting that microRNA profiles may refine subtype assignment and capture plasticity not evident from DNA markers alone ref [103]. Likewise, integration of microRNA expression with MGMT methylation, EGFR/PDGFRA signaling, and stemness programs may improve prediction of alkylator sensitivity or resistance to targeted agents by linking upstream genotype to downstream pathway activity.

Clinically, the most promising use of multi-omic integration is in composite models that combine microRNAs with established classifiers such as IDH status, methylation-based taxonomy, and radiographic phenotypes. DNA methylation profiling has already transformed CNS tumor classification ref [104], while prospective precision-medicine platforms in recurrent glioblastoma have demonstrated the feasibility of assigning matched therapies from molecular data, albeit with modest benefit in unselected populations ref [105], ref [106]. Future biomarker strategies will likely require harmonized modeling across tissue and liquid-biopsy microRNAs together with single-cell and spatial atlases to address intratumoral heterogeneity and temporal evolution ref [107].

subsections.section_title: MicroRNA as Diagnostic, Prognostic, and Predictive Biomarkers in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Challenges in biomarker standardization and validation
subsections.content:
A central barrier to clinical deployment of glioblastoma microRNA biomarkers is the lack of standardization across the entire analytical pipeline. Pre-analytical variables—including ischemia time in resected tissue, hemolysis in plasma/serum, choice of anticoagulant, extracellular vesicle isolation method, and RNA extraction chemistry—can substantially alter measured microRNA abundance and undermine inter-study comparability. These issues are compounded by platform-dependent biases across qRT-PCR, microarray, and small-RNA sequencing, as well as inconsistent normalization strategies in biofluids where stable endogenous controls are difficult to define ref [108], ref [109].

Validation is further complicated by biological heterogeneity intrinsic to glioblastoma. Intratumoral diversity, differences between enhancing core and infiltrative margin, treatment-induced evolution, and variable blood-brain barrier disruption all influence whether a candidate microRNA reflects tumor burden, microenvironmental change, or systemic inflammation. In liquid biopsy studies, contamination by blood-cell–derived microRNAs and inadequate control for hemolysis can generate false-positive signals, while small, single-center retrospective cohorts increase the risk of overfitting and optimistic estimates of classifier performance ref [110], ref [111].

Accordingly, robust translation will require harmonized specimen collection and reporting standards, analytically validated assays with external quality controls, and multi-institutional prospective studies using independent training and validation cohorts. Emerging consensus efforts in extracellular RNA research and liquid biopsy methodology provide a framework for defining minimal experimental information, whereas biomarker development guidelines emphasize the need to separate discovery from clinical qualification and to demonstrate reproducibility, calibration, and incremental value beyond established markers such as MGMT methylation and imaging criteria ref [112], ref [113].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
MicroRNA replacement therapy in glioblastoma is based on restoring tumor-suppressive miRNAs that are frequently downregulated during malignant progression. Rather than targeting a single oncogenic protein, re-expression of these miRNAs can simultaneously modulate cell-cycle control, apoptosis, invasion, stem-like behavior, and therapy response. Early proof-of-principle came from miR-26a, whose enforced expression suppressed gliomagenesis in a mouse model by targeting pathways including PTEN-linked signaling and cell-cycle regulators, illustrating the appeal of network-level correction in this disease ref [114].

Among the best-studied candidates, miR-34a is commonly reduced in glioblastoma and its restoration inhibits proliferation, survival, and invasion, in part through repression of receptor tyrosine kinase and Notch-associated programs ref [115]. Similar tumor-suppressive effects have been reported for miR-128, which restrains self-renewal and proliferation of glioma stem-like cells through Bmi-1 and related stemness pathways ref [24], and for miR-124 and miR-137, which promote neuronal differentiation and induce G1 arrest in high-grade glioma cells ref [60]. These observations support replacement strategies aimed not only at bulk tumor cells but also at stem-like subpopulations implicated in recurrence.

A further rationale comes from miRNAs linked to treatment sensitivity. Restoration of miR-181 family members has been associated with reduced growth and enhanced apoptosis in glioma models ref [116], while miR-7 replacement suppresses EGFR and PI3K/Akt signaling, pathways central to glioblastoma maintenance ref [32]. Collectively, preclinical studies indicate that miRNA mimics can re-establish lost tumor-suppressive circuitry, although durable efficacy will depend on optimized delivery, intracellular release, and avoidance of degradation or unintended gene-network perturbation.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
A complementary therapeutic strategy in glioblastoma is to suppress oncogenic microRNAs (oncomiRs) that sustain proliferation, stemness, invasion, and treatment resistance. Among these, miR-21 is the best-studied target: it is consistently overexpressed in glioblastoma and promotes survival by repressing multiple tumor-suppressive pathways. Early loss-of-function studies showed that antisense inhibition of miR-21 increases apoptosis and reduces tumor cell growth, establishing proof of principle for anti-miR approaches in this disease context [1,2].

Other oncomiRs with therapeutic relevance include the hypoxia-responsive miR-10b and members of the miR-17-92 cluster. miR-10b is largely absent from normal brain but elevated in glioma, where its inhibition suppresses proliferation and invasion, making it an attractive target with a potentially favorable therapeutic window [3]. The miR-17-92 cluster, activated downstream of oncogenic signaling, supports glioblastoma cell-cycle progression and survival, and its blockade has shown anti-tumor effects in preclinical models [4]. More broadly, integrated expression analyses have identified miR-221/222 and related networks as contributors to aggressive phenotypes and resistance programs, further expanding the anti-oncomiR target space [5].

Therapeutically, oncomiR inhibition has been pursued using antisense oligonucleotides, antagomirs, locked nucleic acid (LNA) inhibitors, and miRNA sponges. Preclinical work indicates that such agents can restore derepressed targets, sensitize tumors to apoptosis, and enhance responses to chemo-radiotherapy, although efficacy remains strongly dependent on intracranial delivery and distribution [2,3,6]. Thus, anti-miR strategies are mechanistically compelling in glioblastoma, but their clinical translation hinges on achieving selective, durable target engagement within the brain while limiting systemic and transcriptome-wide off-target effects.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Delivery platforms and blood-brain barrier considerations
subsections.content:
Effective microRNA therapeutics for glioblastoma must overcome rapid nuclease degradation, renal clearance, and limited intratumoral retention, while also traversing the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Although the BBB is partially disrupted in enhancing tumor regions, infiltrative glioblastoma cells often reside behind a relatively intact blood-tumor barrier, making systemic delivery inefficient and spatially heterogeneous. Convection-enhanced delivery has therefore attracted interest because it can bypass the BBB and distribute nucleic acids directly through brain parenchyma, though reflux, variable volume of distribution, and catheter placement remain important practical constraints ref [123].

Nanoparticle-based systems are being developed to improve stability and brain delivery of miRNA mimics or antagomiRs. Lipid nanoparticles, polymeric carriers, and ligand-targeted nanocomplexes can protect cargo and promote receptor-mediated transcytosis across brain endothelium; however, size, surface charge, serum protein adsorption, and uptake by the mononuclear phagocyte system strongly influence performance. More broadly, the design principles for nucleic-acid nanocarriers emphasize balancing circulation time with endosomal escape and tumor penetration, which is especially challenging in the dense, heterogeneous glioblastoma microenvironment ref [124]. Exosome-based delivery is also appealing because endogenous vesicles exhibit relative biocompatibility and can transfer small RNAs across neural compartments; experimental studies have shown that engineered exosomes can deliver therapeutic RNA to the mouse brain after systemic administration ref [125].

BBB-targeting strategies frequently exploit transferrin receptor or other endothelial transport pathways. In a seminal demonstration, systemic delivery of siRNA in transferrin receptor-targeted nanoparticles achieved gene silencing in intracranial tumors, supporting the feasibility of receptor-directed RNA delivery to brain cancers ref [126]. Focused ultrasound combined with microbubbles offers a complementary, noninvasive method for transient BBB opening and has shown promise for enhancing drug accumulation in glioma models and early clinical translation ref [5,6]. Together, these approaches highlight that delivery platform selection is inseparable from BBB biology, route of administration, and the diffuse growth pattern that characterizes glioblastoma.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.subsection_title: Combination strategies with standard and targeted therapies
subsections.content:
Combination approaches are especially attractive in glioblastoma because microRNAs (miRNAs) regulate DNA-damage responses, apoptosis, invasion, and adaptive resistance pathways that limit the efficacy of surgery, radiotherapy, temozolomide (TMZ), and targeted agents. Much of the rationale centers on reversing treatment-induced resistance: for example, restoration of miRNAs with tumor-suppressive activity or inhibition of oncogenic miRNAs can lower anti-apoptotic buffering, impair stem-like phenotypes, and resensitize glioma cells to cytotoxic stress.

The best-developed example is miR-21 inhibition combined with standard therapy. miR-21 is consistently overexpressed in glioblastoma and promotes survival through multiple targets; antisense suppression of miR-21 enhances apoptosis and augments the effects of TMZ in experimental models, while also increasing radiosensitivity in glioma cells ref [129], ref [130]. Similarly, restoring miR-34a has been proposed as a way to complement RTK-directed therapy because miR-34a restrains c-Met, Notch, and cell-cycle programs implicated in resistance, whereas miR-7 suppresses EGFR and PI3K/Akt signaling, supporting its use alongside EGFR-axis inhibition ref [131], ref [32].

Other combinations seek to exploit specific resistance nodes. miR-181d downregulates MGMT, providing a mechanistic basis for synergy with TMZ in MGMT-expressing tumors ref [47]. In parallel, anti-miR strategies against miR-10b can reduce proliferation and survival signaling and may cooperate with cytotoxic or targeted agents in vivo ref [132]. Collectively, these studies suggest that the most promising combinatorial designs will pair miRNA therapeutics with treatments selected according to pathway context—such as MGMT status, EGFR/c-Met activation, or stemness-associated signaling—rather than applying miRNA modulation as a nonspecific add-on ref [129], ref [131], ref [47], ref [132].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
Safety is a central constraint for microRNA therapeutics in glioblastoma because each microRNA can regulate broad gene networks rather than a single target. This pleiotropy is therapeutically attractive but also creates mechanism-based toxicities, including unintended repression of transcripts in normal neurons, astrocytes, endothelial cells, and immune cells. Early systemic experience with the liposomal miR-34a mimic MRX34 highlighted these concerns: although the agent showed pharmacodynamic activity, the phase I trial was terminated after serious immune-mediated adverse events, underscoring that sequence choice, formulation, and innate immune activation are inseparable determinants of safety in microRNA therapy ref [133], ref [134].

Specificity in brain tumors further depends on avoiding both sequence-dependent and sequence-independent off-target effects. Antagomirs, locked nucleic acid inhibitors, and mimics may perturb unrelated RNAs through partial seed matching, saturate endogenous Argonaute/RISC machinery, or trigger Toll-like receptor signaling depending on chemistry and dose ref [135], ref [136]. In glioblastoma, these liabilities are compounded by intratumoral heterogeneity and overlap between malignant and normal glial transcriptional programs, meaning that a microRNA beneficial in one cellular compartment may be deleterious in another. Careful passenger-strand design, chemical modification, dose minimization, and orthotopic toxicology in immunocompetent models are therefore essential.

Delivery systems also shape off-target risk. Cationic lipids and polymeric nanoparticles can induce complement activation, hepatic sequestration, and inflammatory cytokine release, whereas targeted carriers may reduce peripheral exposure but introduce new immunogenicity or biodistribution issues ref [137]. More broadly, experience across oligonucleotide therapeutics shows that hybridization-dependent off-target binding and tissue accumulation must be anticipated early through transcriptome-wide profiling and long-term safety studies ref [138]. For glioblastoma, the most credible translational path will likely pair tumor-restricted delivery with rigorous molecular deconvolution of on-target versus bystander effects in the brain and peripheral organs.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Targeting of MicroRNA in Glioblastoma
subsections.content:
Preclinical work has provided proof-of-concept that both microRNA restoration and anti-microRNA strategies can suppress glioblastoma growth, stem-like behavior, and therapeutic resistance. Early studies showed that reconstitution of tumor-suppressive miRNAs such as miR-34a inhibits proliferation, survival signaling, and glioma stem cell phenotypes, whereas targeting oncomiRs including miR-21 reduces invasion and promotes apoptosis in orthotopic models ref [33], ref [139]. Likewise, miR-10b emerged as a particularly compelling dependency in malignant glioma, with its inhibition producing marked antitumor effects across established lines and patient-derived cells ref [75].

Translationally, the field has advanced from mechanistic validation toward platform-enabled delivery in clinically relevant models. Systemic or local administration of oligonucleotide inhibitors, viral constructs, and nanoparticle formulations has demonstrated that therapeutic modulation of miRNA networks is feasible in intracranial tumors, although efficacy remains closely tied to delivery efficiency and intratumoral distribution. An important milestone was the first-in-human development of a miR-34 mimic, which established the clinical tractability of miRNA therapeutics even though immune-related toxicities limited progress and underscored the gap between antitumor rationale and safe systemic implementation ref [133]. In glioblastoma specifically, preclinical studies using targeted nanoparticles or convection-enhanced approaches have shown improved intracranial delivery of anti-miR-21 or related payloads, supporting continued optimization of route and carrier design ref [140], ref [141].

Overall, translational progress in glioblastoma remains promising but incomplete. The strongest evidence supports miRNA modulation as a network-level strategy capable of simultaneously affecting proliferation, stemness, invasion, and treatment response; however, reproducibility in heterogeneous patient-derived models, scalable brain delivery, and rigorous toxicology remain the key barriers to clinical entry. These issues are now shaping next-generation studies that integrate molecular stratification and combination therapy rather than relying on single-agent miRNA activity alone ref [75], ref [141], ref [142].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Advances, Current Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Experimental models for studying microRNA in glioblastoma
subsections.content:
Experimental model choice strongly shapes conclusions about microRNA function in glioblastoma. Conventional serum-grown cell lines such as U87 and U251 enabled early gain- and loss-of-function studies, including landmark work showing that miR-21 promotes glioma growth and suppresses apoptosis ref [143]. However, prolonged culture in serum alters lineage state, genotype, and drug response, limiting their ability to represent patient tumors. More recent studies therefore favor patient-derived glioblastoma stem-like cells propagated under neurosphere conditions, which better preserve tumor-initiating capacity and clinically relevant microRNA programs, including hypoxia-responsive networks linked to stemness and angiogenesis ref [68], ref [86].

In vivo systems are essential because microRNA phenotypes are highly context dependent. Orthotopic xenografts reproduce brain-specific invasion, vascular interactions, and blood-brain barrier constraints more faithfully than subcutaneous implants, and they were central to demonstrating tumor-suppressive effects of miR-128 and miR-34a in glioblastoma models ref [34], ref [144]. Genetically engineered mouse models add an immunocompetent setting and permit interrogation of microRNA function during tumor evolution, although species differences in target sites and developmental timing complicate direct translation. Emerging organoid and cerebral assembloid platforms further extend this toolkit by enabling analysis of glioblastoma–microenvironment crosstalk and cellular plasticity in human tissue contexts ref [145].

A major methodological priority is to integrate models rather than rely on any single platform. Findings from 2D cultures should be validated in patient-derived stem-like cells and orthotopic models, ideally with matched molecular characterization and assessment of extracellular vesicle-mediated microRNA transfer, which is increasingly recognized as biologically relevant in glioblastoma ref [50]. Such multi-model designs are especially important for distinguishing cell-intrinsic microRNA effects from those arising through stromal, immune, or vascular interactions.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Advances, Current Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
MicroRNA profiling in glioblastoma has progressed from candidate-based assays to genome-scale platforms. Early studies relied heavily on microarrays, which enabled the first disease-associated signatures but were limited by cross-hybridization, narrow dynamic range, and dependence on prior annotation. Quantitative RT-PCR arrays improved sensitivity for focused panels, whereas small-RNA sequencing expanded detection to low-abundance species, isomiRs, and previously unannotated transcripts, while also reducing platform-specific bias when library preparation and normalization are carefully controlled ref [146], ref [147]. More recently, digital counting approaches such as NanoString have been attractive for formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded specimens because they avoid enzymatic amplification and can perform robustly on degraded RNA ref [148].

Technology choice is especially consequential in glioblastoma because biospecimens vary substantially across bulk tumor, microdissected niches, patient-derived stem-like cells, serum, cerebrospinal fluid, and extracellular vesicles. Pre-analytical variables including ischemia time, hemolysis, RNA extraction chemistry, and exosome isolation method can alter apparent miRNA abundance as much as biological state, complicating cross-study comparisons ref [149], ref [150]. Accordingly, profiling studies increasingly combine discovery by sequencing or multiplex counting with orthogonal validation by stem-loop RT-qPCR, northern blotting for size confirmation, and in situ hybridization to preserve spatial context within the tumor microenvironment ref [147], ref [151].

A major methodological challenge is normalization. The frequent use of small nuclear RNAs such as U6 as universal controls is problematic in biofluids and unstable across conditions; global mean strategies, spike-ins, or empirically validated endogenous reference miRNAs are often preferable depending on specimen type ref [152]. Future glioblastoma studies will benefit from single-cell and spatial transcriptomic adaptations that better resolve cell-state-specific miRNA expression, but these approaches must still be anchored to rigorous validation frameworks before candidate biomarkers or mechanisms can be considered reproducible.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Advances, Current Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Computational prediction has become essential for moving from lists of dysregulated microRNAs in glioblastoma to mechanistic hypotheses. Because sequence-based target prediction alone yields many false positives, most studies now integrate seed matching and conservation with expression anticorrelation, pathway enrichment, and experimentally supported interaction resources such as miRTarBase and CLIP-informed datasets. Foundational algorithms including TargetScan and miRanda remain widely used, but their outputs are most informative when filtered through glioblastoma-specific transcriptomic context and validated against perturbation data rather than treated as universal target sets [1,2].

Network-based analyses further recognize that microRNAs act as distributed regulators of oncogenic programs rather than one-miRNA/one-target switches. Integrative frameworks combining miRNA and mRNA profiles from cohorts such as TCGA have been used to infer regulatory modules linked to proneural, classical, and mesenchymal states, highlighting convergence on pathways controlling invasion, stemness, hypoxia, and therapy resistance [3,4]. More recently, graph-based and single-cell-informed approaches have emphasized that inferred miRNA-mRNA edges are state dependent and can differ across malignant cells, glioma stem-like compartments, and the tumor microenvironment, limiting the interpretability of bulk-tissue networks [5].

Current priorities are therefore methodological as much as biological: benchmarking prediction tools, incorporating Argonaute binding and RNA abundance constraints, and modeling competing endogenous RNA effects without overinterpreting correlation structure. Causal network reconstruction from perturbational datasets, together with multimodal and spatial transcriptomic integration, should provide more reliable maps of microRNA-centered circuitry in glioblastoma and better support biomarker prioritization and combination therapy design [6,7].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Advances, Current Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
A central limitation in microRNA studies of glioblastoma is that apparent “driver” miRNA programs are strongly shaped by interpatient heterogeneity. Large-scale genomic analyses established that glioblastoma comprises molecularly distinct transcriptional subtypes and variable combinations of EGFR, PDGFRA, NF1, PTEN, and TP53 alterations, implying that the phenotypic effect of a given miRNA depends on the surrounding regulatory landscape rather than on a fixed, tumor-wide function alone ref [1], ref [158]. This is compounded by extensive intratumoral diversity, including coexisting cellular states with stem-like, proliferative, and mesenchymal features, which can produce different miRNA expression patterns even within the same lesion ref [3].

Context dependence is also imposed by the tumor microenvironment. Single-cell analyses have shown that neoplastic programs are intertwined with region-specific hypoxia, immune infiltration, and stromal interactions, all of which can reshape miRNA biogenesis, secretion, and target engagement ref [3], ref [159]. Moreover, glioma stem-like cells differ from more differentiated tumor cells in miRNA networks governing self-renewal, invasion, and therapy response, helping explain why findings from bulk tissue or standard serum-grown lines often fail to generalize across patients ref [24].

These observations argue against interpreting any miRNA as universally oncogenic or tumor suppressive in glioblastoma. Future studies should therefore stratify cohorts by molecular subtype, treatment status, anatomic sampling region, and cellular composition, and should integrate miRNA profiling with matched single-cell or spatial transcriptomic data to identify context-specific regulatory circuits and clinically robust biomarkers ref [159], ref [160].

subsections.section_title: Methodological Advances, Current Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Reproducibility, standardization, and study design limitations
subsections.content:
A persistent obstacle in microRNA–glioblastoma research is limited reproducibility across cohorts and platforms. Differences in tissue procurement, ischemic time, tumor cellularity, necrosis, and admixture with non-neoplastic brain can substantially alter measured small-RNA abundance, while divergent normalization strategies and low-input protocols further complicate cross-study comparisons. The broader miRNA field has shown that pre-analytical handling and analytical workflow strongly influence profiling results, underscoring the need for explicit standard operating procedures and transparent reporting ref [161], ref [162]. In glioblastoma, molecular subclassification and sample purity are themselves variable, making it difficult to distinguish biological signal from technical or compositional noise ref [163].

Study design limitations also remain common. Many reports rely on small, single-center retrospective series, use unmatched controls such as epileptic or peritumoral tissue, and validate only a few candidate miRNAs without independent external cohorts. In addition, reliance on established serum-containing cell lines can produce findings that are poorly representative of patient tumors; genomic and phenotypic drift in long-term glioma cell culture is well documented ref [164]. Similar concerns apply to circulating miRNA studies, where hemolysis, platelet contamination, and inconsistent RNA isolation methods can create artifactual signatures unless rigorously controlled ref [165].

Future progress will require harmonized biospecimen collection, minimum metadata standards, orthogonal validation by qRT-PCR or digital PCR, and routine use of multi-institutional datasets with predefined endpoints. Adherence to reporting frameworks for molecular prognostic studies and transparent handling of normalization, batch correction, and multiple testing would improve comparability and reduce false discovery ref [166], ref [167]. More systematic inclusion of patient-derived models, spatially resolved sampling, and prospective validation should help establish which miRNA associations are robust enough for mechanistic inference or clinical translation.

subsections.section_title: Methodological Advances, Current Limitations, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Emerging frontiers and future research priorities
subsections.content:
A major frontier is the shift from bulk correlations to spatially and temporally resolved microRNA biology. Single-cell and single-nucleus atlases have shown that glioblastoma comprises dynamic cellular states embedded within distinct immune and vascular niches, implying that microRNA function will be highly state- and location-dependent rather than uniform across tumors ref [168], ref [169]. Future studies should therefore integrate single-cell transcriptomics with spatial profiling and matched small-RNA measurements to identify microRNA programs that govern lineage plasticity, therapy adaptation, and microenvironmental crosstalk.

Another priority is to move beyond tumor-cell-intrinsic models and define extracellular and intercellular microRNA signaling. Extracellular vesicles released by glioblastoma can transfer RNA cargo to endothelial and immune cells and have been proposed as minimally invasive biomarkers, but their functional specificity, cellular origin, and kinetics remain incompletely resolved ref [50], ref [170]. This will require rigorously standardized biofluid processing, orthogonal validation of vesicle-associated microRNAs, and longitudinal sampling before, during, and after therapy.

Therapeutically, the field is being reshaped by RNA engineering and precision delivery. Clinical experience with microRNA replacement has highlighted both feasibility and the importance of immune toxicity, biodistribution, and patient selection ref [133]. In parallel, nucleic-acid and CRISPR-based editing strategies are creating opportunities to perturb microRNA loci and networks with greater specificity than earlier mimics or antagomirs ref [171]. A realistic future agenda is to combine these tools with robust molecular stratification and response biomarkers, while embedding studies in reproducible preclinical frameworks that better capture glioblastoma heterogeneity ref [7].
